How to Use This Book

This book covers Section A of MTE 4011, which is Atia Ma'am's part of the course. Every chapter follows her six lecture files (S1–S6) and has three layers:

  1. Theory: each slide idea rewritten as a complete, exam-ready explanation, with the missing “see lecture note” derivations filled in.
  2. Worked lecture examples: the numerical examples shown on the slides (golf ID3, green/yellow Naïve Bayes, soft-margin SVM, the 2-2-2 backpropagation network) are fully recomputed.
  3. Solved past questions: every Section A question from the 2022, 2023 and 2024 term finals, quoted word for word and then answered. Numericals start with a Given Data block and show every arithmetic step. Derivations are line by line, with the rule used at each step.

1. Introduction to Machine Learning ★★★

1.1 What is Machine Learning?

Definitions (write both)
Herbert Simon: “Learning is any process by which a system improves performance from experience.”

Tom Mitchell (1998): Machine Learning is the study of algorithms that improve their performance P at some task T with experience E. A well-defined learning task is given by the triple ⟨P, T, E⟩.

If performance P increases as experience E increases, learning has occurred. If the system only reproduces what it has seen, without improving on new cases, it is memorising, not learning.

In simple terms, machine learning is the branch of artificial intelligence in which computers learn patterns and relationships from data and use them to make predictions or decisions on new data, without being explicitly programmed with hand-written rules for the task.

1.1.1 “Machine” and “Learning” separately

Machine: the hardware or computational system that runs the algorithms and models: a computer, a mobile device, a cloud server, or an embedded controller. It must have enough processing power and memory to run the learning algorithms.

Learning: a computational process that improves performance based on experience. It is the process by which the machine gets better at a task over time without being explicitly programmed to do so. In ML the experience is the training data, and the algorithms find patterns and relationships in that data.

1.2 Defining the Learning Task (T, P, E)

ProblemTask TPerformance PExperience E
(i) Handwriting recognitionRecognise and classify handwritten words in imagesPercent of words correctly classifiedA dataset of handwritten words with given classifications
(ii) Autonomous drivingDrive on highways using vision sensorsAverage distance travelled before an errorA sequence of images and steering commands recorded while observing a human driver
(iii) ChessPlay chessPercent of games won against opponentsPractice games played against itself
(iv) Spam filter (extra)Classify e-mails as spam / not spamPercent of e-mails correctly classifiedE-mails labelled by users
(v) Robot arm (mechatronics, extra)Pick objects of varying shapeSuccessful grasp rateRecorded grasp attempts with success/failure labels

1.3 Why Machine Learning? Why Should Machines Learn?

Early “intelligent” systems used hand-coded if/else rules. For example, a spam filter might use a blacklist of words. Hand-crafted rules work only when humans understand the process well, and they have two major disadvantages:

  1. The decision logic is specific to one domain and task. Changing the task even slightly may mean rewriting the whole system.
  2. Designing the rules needs a deep understanding of how a human expert makes the decision.

Example (face detection): computers “see” an image as a grid of pixel numbers, which is very different from how humans perceive a face. It is basically impossible to write rules describing a face in pixel terms, and face detection was unsolved until about 2001. With ML, simply giving the algorithm a large collection of face images is enough for it to learn the characteristics that identify a face.

Learning is used (important) when…
  • Human expertise does not exist: e.g. navigating on Mars.
  • Humans cannot explain their expertise: e.g. speech recognition.
  • The solution changes over time: e.g. routing on a computer network.
  • The solution must be adapted to particular cases: e.g. user biometrics.
  • The environment is unknown: the designer cannot foresee everything.
  • It is a useful system-construction method: expose the system to reality rather than trying to write everything down.

1.4 Applications of Machine Learning

  1. Retail: study of consumer behaviour, recommendations.
  2. Finance: credit scoring, fraud detection, stock-market analysis.
  3. Manufacturing: optimisation, control and troubleshooting.
  4. Medicine: medical diagnosis (e.g. benign vs malignant tumour).
  5. Telecommunications: call-pattern analysis for network optimisation and quality of service.
  6. Science and the web: analysing huge data in physics, astronomy and biology; web search.
  7. Artificial intelligence: systems that adapt to change without the designer foreseeing every situation.
  8. Vision, speech recognition and robotics.
  9. Autonomous vehicles: steering correctly on a variety of roads.
  10. Games: chess, backgammon, Go (AlphaGo).

1.5 Types of Learning

TypeGivenDefinitionExamples (lecture)
Supervised (inductive)Training data + desired outputs (labels)The model is trained on labelled data, where each input is paired with the correct output. It learns to map inputs to outputs by minimising prediction error.Zip code from handwritten digits; benign vs malignant tumour from a medical image; credit-card fraud detection
UnsupervisedTraining data only (no labels)The algorithm finds patterns, structure or groupings in unlabelled data with no predefined outputs.Customer segmentation (“parents”, “bookworms”, “gamers”); detecting abnormal access patterns to a website
Semi-supervisedTraining data + a few labelsCombines a small amount of labelled data with a large amount of unlabelled data. It improves accuracy while reducing labelling cost.Text/news classification; image classification; medical imaging; anomaly detection
ReinforcementRewards from a sequence of actionsAn agent interacts with an environment, takes actions, receives rewards or penalties, and learns by trial and error to maximise the cumulative reward.Robot navigating a maze; AlphaGo; self-driving decisions; recommendation systems; industrial control

1.6 ML vs Classical Statistics; AI vs ML vs DL

AspectClassical statistical methodsMachine learning
Main goalInference: explain relationships and test hypothesesPrediction and generalisation to unseen data
AssumptionsStrong: a known distribution (e.g. normal), linearity, independenceFew: learns the functional form from data
Data size and dimensionSmall–medium data, few variablesScales to big, high-dimensional data (images, text, sensors)

InterpretabilityHigh for rule systemsMedium (trees are interpretable)Low (“black box”)

1.7 Common Data Types in ML

  • Numerical (quantitative): continuous (temperature, price, voltage) and discrete (count of items).
  • Categorical (qualitative): nominal, with no order (colour, outlook = sunny/rainy); ordinal, with an order (low/medium/high, grades); binary (yes/no, 0/1).
  • Text: e-mails and reviews (needs tokenisation or embeddings).
  • Image and video: pixel arrays.
  • Audio / signal: speech, vibration signals from machines.
  • Time-series: sensor readings over time, stock prices.
  • Structured vs unstructured: tables vs raw media. Labelled vs unlabelled data (with or without target values).

1.8 Solved Past Questions

2024 · Q1(a)Q1.1 — Define “Machine Learning”. Define the learning task for three examples. Why is learning important for machines?10Topic: ML definition · P-T-E

Definition. Machine learning is the study of algorithms that improve their performance P at some task T with experience E (Tom Mitchell, 1998). A well-defined learning task is the triple ⟨P, T, E⟩. If P improves as E increases, the system has learned. Otherwise it has only memorised. Equivalently (Herbert Simon), learning is any process by which a system improves its performance from experience.

Learning tasks for three examples:

ExampleTPE
Handwriting recognitionRecognise and classify handwritten words in images% of words correctly classifiedDatabase of handwritten words with labels
Autonomous drivingDrive on highways using vision sensorsAverage distance travelled before an errorImages and steering commands recorded from a human driver
ChessPlay chess% of games won against opponentsPractice games against itself

Why learning is important for machines: (1) Hand-coded rules are domain-specific and need expert knowledge. A small change in the task can mean rewriting the system. (2) Some tasks cannot be written as rules at all, such as face detection from pixels. (3) Learning is needed when human expertise does not exist (Mars navigation), when humans cannot explain their expertise (speech recognition), when the solution changes over time (network routing), when it must be adapted to individuals (biometrics), and in unknown environments. (4) Learning is a practical way to build systems: expose them to reality instead of writing everything down.

Source lectureAtia Ma'am · S1 – Introduction (MTE 4011 S1.pdf, pp. 4–8)
2022 · Q1(a)Q1.2 — What is Machine Learning? Briefly discuss some practical applications of Machine Learning in Mechatronics Engineering.10Topic: ML definition · applications

Machine learning is a branch of AI in which a system improves its performance P on a task T with experience E, by learning patterns from data instead of following explicitly programmed rules (Mitchell). A trained model can generalise, meaning it makes accurate predictions on new, unseen data.

Applications in mechatronics engineering:

  1. Predictive maintenance and fault diagnosis: classifiers (SVM, random forest, neural networks) trained on vibration, current and temperature data detect bearing or gear faults and predict remaining useful life before a breakdown.
  2. Robotics: learning grasping, path planning and manipulation. Reinforcement learning lets a robot learn to walk or navigate a maze by reward and penalty.
  3. Autonomous vehicles and drones: lane and object detection from cameras, steering commands learned from a human driver, sensor fusion.
  4. Machine vision in manufacturing: defect detection on production lines, sorting parts, reading labels (OCR), quality inspection.
  5. Intelligent control: neural-network and learning-based controllers for nonlinear plants, adaptive tuning of PID gains, optimising energy use in industrial processes.
  6. Sensor calibration and soft sensing: regression models estimate hard-to-measure variables (e.g. tool wear) from easily measured signals.
  7. Human–machine interaction: speech and gesture recognition, EMG-controlled prosthetic arms, driver-drowsiness detection.
  8. Smart manufacturing (Industry 4.0): demand forecasting, process optimisation, anomaly detection in IoT data.
Source lectureAtia Ma'am · S1 – Introduction (MTE 4011 S1.pdf, p. 4); S1 – Introduction (MTE 4011 S1.pdf, p. 9) — Mechatronics-specific applications not listed in slides
2024 · Q1(c)Q1.3 — Describe the positive aspects of machine learning over classical statistical methods. Distinguish between artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning.15Topic: ML vs statistics · AI/ML/DL

Positive aspects of ML over classical statistical methods:

  1. Prediction-focused: ML aims to generalise to unseen data and is judged on test performance. Statistics mainly aims at inference about parameters.
  2. Fewer assumptions: statistical models often assume linearity, normality and independence. ML learns the functional form, including complex non-linear relationships, directly from data.
  3. Handles big and high-dimensional data: thousands of features and millions of samples (gradient-based training works when n>106n > 10^6n>106).
  4. Unstructured data: images, audio, text and signals can be learned from directly, especially with deep learning.
  5. Automation and adaptivity: models can be retrained automatically as data changes (online learning), and features can be learned instead of hand-crafted.
  6. Solves problems with no known rules: face detection, speech recognition.
  7. Wide range of tools: trees, SVMs, ensembles and neural networks for classification, regression, clustering and control.

AI vs ML vs DL: draw Fig. 1.1 (DL ⊂ ML ⊂ AI) and write the comparison table from §1.6. In short: AI is the broad goal of making machines act intelligently, by any means including rules and search. ML is the subset of AI in which machines learn from data and improve with experience. DL is the subset of ML that uses deep, multi-layer neural networks to learn features automatically from raw data. DL needs large data and GPUs but achieves state-of-the-art results in vision and language.

Source lectureAtia Ma'am · S1 – Introduction (MTE 4011 S1.pdf, pp. 6–7) — Only ML vs hand-coded rules; statistics and AI/ML/DL comparison not in slides

2022 · Q3(d)Q1.5 — What are the common data types in machine learning?05Topic: Data types

(1) Numerical: continuous (temperature, price) and discrete (counts). (2) Categorical: nominal (colour, outlook), ordinal (low < medium < high), binary (yes/no). (3) Text (documents, e-mails). (4) Image/video (pixel arrays). (5) Audio/signal (speech, vibration). (6) Time-series (sensor streams). Data may also be classed as structured (tables) vs unstructured (media), and labelled vs unlabelled. Categorical data is usually converted to numbers (label or one-hot encoding), and numerical data is often scaled before training.

2. Regression and Optimisation ★★★

2.1 Regression and Classification Tasks

Regression and classification are the two fundamental types of supervised learning problems.

AspectRegressionClassification
DefinitionPredicting a continuous numerical value from input featuresPredicting a discrete label or category for an input, based on patterns learned from labelled data
OutputReal number y∈Ry\in\mathbb{R}y∈R (e.g. 23.7 °C)Class label y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\}y∈{0,1} or {C1,…,CK}\{C_1,\dots,C_K\}{C1​,…,CK​}
ExamplesTemperature, stock price, energy consumption, house priceSpam detection, disease diagnosis, fault/no fault
AlgorithmsLinear, polynomial, SVR, regression trees, random forestLogistic regression, k-NN, SVM, decision trees, random forest, neural networks
Loss / metricMSE, MAE, R2R^2R2Cross-entropy; accuracy, precision, recall
DecisionFits a best-fit line/curve through the dataFinds a decision boundary between classes

2.2 Linear Regression

Regression is a technique for modelling and analysing numerical data. It exploits the relationship between two or more variables so that knowing some of them tells us about another. It is used for prediction, estimation, hypothesis testing and modelling causal relationships. Lingo: YYY is the dependent / outcome / response variable; X1,X2,…X_1,X_2,\dotsX1​,X2​,… are independent / predictor / feature variables.

Linear regression model
Linear regression models the relationship between a dependent variable YYY and independent variables X1,…,XnX_1,\dots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ as linear: Y=β0+β1X1+β2X2+⋯+βnXn+εY=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\beta_2X_2+\cdots+\beta_nX_n+\varepsilonY=β0​+β1​X1​+β2​X2​+⋯+βn​Xn​+ε β0\beta_0β0​ = intercept, β1,…,βn\beta_1,\dots,\beta_nβ1​,…,βn​ = regression coefficients, ε\varepsilonε = error term, assumed ε∼N(0,σ2)\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)ε∼N(0,σ2).

Why linear? We would like Y=f(X1,X2,X3)Y=f(X_1,X_2,X_3)Y=f(X1​,X2​,X3​), but there is usually not enough data to estimate an arbitrary fff. So we assume a restricted form, the simplest being linear.

Linear regression is a probabilistic model. A deterministic relation y=β0+β1xy=\beta_0+\beta_1xy=β0​+β1​x (slope β1=Δy/Δx\beta_1=\Delta y/\Delta xβ1​=Δy/Δx) cannot describe real data, which scatter around a line. The linear probabilistic model states that there exist parameters β0,β1,σ2\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2β0​,β1​,σ2 such that, for any fixed xxx, y=β0+β1x+εy=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\varepsilony=β0​+β1​x+ε with ε∼N(0,σ2)\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)ε∼N(0,σ2). The line y=β0+β1xy=\beta_0+\beta_1xy=β0​+β1​x is the true regression line, and the εi\varepsilon_iεi​ are the vertical deviations of the points from it.

2.2.1 Predicted values, residuals, SSE and R²

  • Predicted (fitted) values: y^i=β^0+β^1xi\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_iy^​i​=β^​0​+β^​1​xi​.
  • Residuals: ei=yi−y^ie_i=y_i-\hat y_iei​=yi​−y^​i​ (observed minus predicted).
  • Error sum of squares: SSE=∑i=1nei2=∑i=1n(yi−y^i)2SSE=\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_i^2=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat y_i)^2SSE=∑i=1n​ei2​=∑i=1n​(yi​−y^​i​)2: the variability left unexplained by the regression.
  • Variance estimate: σ^2=SSEn−2\hat\sigma^2=\dfrac{SSE}{n-2}σ^2=n−2SSE​ (two parameters estimated in simple regression).
  • Total sum of squares: SST=∑i=1n(yi−yˉ)2SST=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar y)^2SST=∑i=1n​(yi​−yˉ​)2: the total variance in yyy.
  • Coefficient of determination: R2=1−SSESSTR^2=1-\dfrac{SSE}{SST}R2=1−SSTSSE​. The higher, the better the model fits (0 to 1). It measures the accuracy of the regression and, for simple regression, equals r2r^2r2, the square of the correlation coefficient. It therefore measures how strong the linear relationship is.

2.2.2 Multiple linear regression

This extends the model to two or more independent variables: y=β0+β1x1+β2x2+⋯+βnxn+εy=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+\dots+\beta_nx_n+\varepsilony=β0​+β1​x1​+β2​x2​+⋯+βn​xn​+ε. Example: Expression = Baseline + Age + Height + Gender + Error, or house price from size, number of rooms and so on.

2.2.3 Polynomial regression

Definition
Polynomial regression is an extension of linear regression that models the relationship between xxx and yyy as an nnn-th-degree polynomial: y=β0+β1x+β2x2+β3x3+⋯+βnxn+εy=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\beta_3x^3+\cdots+\beta_nx^n+\varepsilony=β0​+β1​x+β2​x2+β3​x3+⋯+βn​xn+ε Linear regression fits a straight line. Polynomial regression fits a curve to capture more complex relationships.

Why use it? (1) It captures non-linear trends, i.e. curvature that a straight line cannot model. (2) It is flexible: with enough degree it approximates complex functions. (3) It is still linear in the parameters βi\beta_iβi​, so ordinary least squares (the normal equation or gradient descent) still applies. Just set x1=x,x2=x2,…x_1=x, x_2=x^2,\dotsx1​=x,x2​=x2,… and run multiple linear regression. Caution: a very high degree overfits (see Chapter 5).

2.2.4 Assumptions of linear regression

  1. The underlying relationship between XXX and YYY is linear.
  2. Error values are statistically independent.
  3. Errors are normally distributed for any given value of xxx.
  4. Errors have constant variance (homoscedasticity).
  5. Hence the output yyy is normally distributed about the regression line.
  6. Features are independent of each other: no multicollinearity.

2.2.5 Linear and non-linear problems

A problem is linear when the output can be modelled as a linear combination of the input features (regression), or when the classes can be separated by a straight line or hyperplane (classification, “linearly separable”). Example: salary vs years of experience; AND/OR gates. A problem is non-linear when the relationship is curved or the classes cannot be separated by any single hyperplane. Example: the XOR problem, concentric circles of classes, the stress–strain curve beyond yield, image recognition. Non-linear problems need non-linear models (polynomial features, kernel SVM, decision trees, neural networks with non-linear activations) or feature transformations that make them linear in a new space.

2.3 Training = Optimisation: the MSE Cost

Training means finding the parameters of f(x)=wx+bf(x)=wx+bf(x)=wx+b (or hθ(x)=θTxh_\theta(x)=\theta^Txhθ​(x)=θTx) that fit the dataset best. The Mean Squared Error measures the difference between the labels yyy and the predictions h(x)h(x)h(x): MSE=1m∑i=1m(yi−h(xi))2,J(θ)=12m∑i=1m(hθ(xi)−yi)2MSE=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\big(y_i-h(x_i)\big)^2,\qquad J(\theta)=\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\big(h_\theta(x_i)-y_i\big)^2MSE=m1​i=1∑m​(yi​−h(xi​))2,J(θ)=2m1​i=1∑m​(hθ​(xi​)−yi​)2 A small MSE means predictions are close to the actual values. A large MSE means they differ. The factor ½ in JJJ just cancels the 2 produced when differentiating. There are two ways to minimise it: (1) the design-matrix approach (linear algebra, a closed form) and (2) gradient descent (a first-order iterative method).

2.4.1 When XᵀX is non-invertible

Causes: (1) redundant features, i.e. linearly dependent columns (e.g. size in m² and size in ft², or x3=2x1x_3=2x_1x3​=2x1​); (2) too many features compared with examples (m≤nm\le nm≤n).

Remedies: (a) delete redundant features or reduce their number (feature selection, PCA); (b) use regularisation (ridge), which keeps all features but shrinks the parameters; (c) use the Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse θ=X+Y\theta=X^{+}Yθ=X+Y (numpy pinv), which gives the minimum-norm least-squares solution.

Ridge (regularised) normal equation
Minimise J(θ)=12m[(Xθ−Y)T(Xθ−Y)+λ θTLθ]J(\theta)=\dfrac{1}{2m}\Big[(X\theta-Y)^T(X\theta-Y)+\lambda\,\theta^TL\theta\Big]J(θ)=2m1​[(Xθ−Y)T(Xθ−Y)+λθTLθ] with L=diag(0,1,…,1)L=\mathrm{diag}(0,1,\dots,1)L=diag(0,1,…,1) (the intercept is not penalised). Gradient =0=0=0 gives θ=(XTX+λL)−1XTY\theta=(X^TX+\lambda L)^{-1}X^TYθ=(XTX+λL)−1XTY For λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 the matrix XTX+λLX^TX+\lambda LXTX+λL is always invertible. Regularisation keeps all features but reduces the size of the parameters, giving a simpler hypothesis that is less prone to overfitting. It works well when many features each contribute a little to predicting yyy.

2.5 Gradient Descent

Algorithm
Gradient descent is a first-order iterative method for finding the minimum of a function. Starting from an initial guess, it repeatedly steps opposite to the gradient (the direction of steepest descent): repeat until convergence: θj:=θj−α∂J(θ)∂θj(all j updated simultaneously)\text{repeat until convergence: }\quad \theta_j:=\theta_j-\alpha\frac{\partial J(\theta)}{\partial\theta_j}\quad(\text{all } j \text{ updated simultaneously})repeat until convergence: θj​:=θj​−α∂θj​∂J(θ)​(all j updated simultaneously) For linear regression: ∂J∂θj=1m∑i=1m(hθ(xi)−yi)xj,i\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial\theta_j}=\dfrac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\big(h_\theta(x_i)-y_i\big)x_{j,i}∂θj​∂J​=m1​∑i=1m​(hθ​(xi​)−yi​)xj,i​ (with x0,i=1x_{0,i}=1x0,i​=1). In vector form: θ:=θ−αmXT(Xθ−Y)\theta:=\theta-\dfrac{\alpha}{m}X^T(X\theta-Y)θ:=θ−mα​XT(Xθ−Y).
Derivation of the partial derivative. J=12m∑i(hθ(xi)−yi)2J=\frac{1}{2m}\sum_i(h_\theta(x_i)-y_i)^2J=2m1​∑i​(hθ​(xi​)−yi​)2. By the chain rule, ∂J∂θj=12m∑i2(hθ(xi)−yi)⋅∂hθ(xi)∂θj\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial\theta_j}=\frac{1}{2m}\sum_i 2(h_\theta(x_i)-y_i)\cdot\dfrac{\partial h_\theta(x_i)}{\partial\theta_j}∂θj​∂J​=2m1​∑i​2(hθ​(xi​)−yi​)⋅∂θj​∂hθ​(xi​)​, and ∂hθ(xi)∂θj=xj,i\dfrac{\partial h_\theta(x_i)}{\partial\theta_j}=x_{j,i}∂θj​∂hθ​(xi​)​=xj,i​ because hhh is linear in θ\thetaθ. The 2 cancels the ½.
[KEY IDENTITY]Chain rule: ddθu2=2ududθ\dfrac{d}{d\theta}u^2 = 2u\dfrac{du}{d\theta}dθd​u2=2udθdu​.
Worked iteration (data of §2.4.2, α=0.1\alpha=0.1α=0.1, start θ=(0,0)\theta=(0,0)θ=(0,0)): all predictions are 0, so the errors are (−2,−3,−5)(-2,-3,-5)(−2,−3,−5).

[INTUITION]A negative gradient means increasing θ lowers the cost, so the update increases θ.

2.5.1 Learning rate α

Small α: small steps toward the minimum, so it takes more time (many iterations) to converge, but it is stable. Large α: big steps, faster at first but less accurate. It may overshoot the minimum, oscillate or even diverge (cost increases). A good α is found by plotting JJJ against the iteration number and trying values such as 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1 …, or by using learning-rate schedules and adaptive optimisers (Adam, RMSprop).

2.7 Solved Past Questions

2023 · Q1(a)Q2.1 — Define classification, regression, and logistic regression in short. Differentiate between the concepts: “classification vs. regression” and “regression vs. logistic regression”.12Topic: Task types

Classification: a supervised learning task that predicts a discrete label or category for an input, based on patterns learned from labelled training data (e.g. spam / not spam). Regression: a supervised learning task that predicts a continuous numerical value from the input features (e.g. temperature, house price). Logistic regression: despite its name, a classification algorithm. It passes a linear combination of the features through the sigmoid, p(x)=11+e−(b0+b1x1+⋯+bnxn)p(x)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-(b_0+b_1x_1+\dots+b_nx_n)}}p(x)=1+e−(b0​+b1​x1​+⋯+bn​xn​)1​, to output the probability that an input belongs to class 1, and thresholds it (usually at 0.5) to predict the class.

Classification vs regression: write the table of §2.1 (output type discrete vs continuous; boundary vs best-fit line; cross-entropy/accuracy vs MSE/R²; examples).

Regression (linear) vs logistic regression:

PointLinear regressionLogistic regression
Problem solvedRegression: continuous outputClassification: binary (0/1) output
Modely=β0+β1x+…y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\dotsy=β0​+β1​x+… (straight line/plane)p=σ(β0+β1x+… )p=\sigma(\beta_0+\beta_1x+\dots)p=σ(β0​+β1​x+…) (S-shaped sigmoid)
Output range−∞-\infty−∞ to +∞+\infty+∞0 to 1 (a probability)
LinearityOutput linear in the parametersThe logit ln⁡p1−p\ln\frac{p}{1-p}ln1−pp​ is linear in the parameters (a generalised linear model)
Cost / fittingLeast squares (MSE); closed form availableMaximum likelihood (log-loss); iterative (gradient descent, Newton–Raphson)
OutliersSensitive: the line shifts a lotSigmoid saturates, so it is much less sensitive
Error assumptionNormally distributed errorsBernoulli-distributed output
ExamplePredict the credit-card balancePredict whether a customer will default (yes/no)

Logistic regression fixes this with the sigmoid, which squashes the output into [0, 1].”

2024 · Q1(b)Q2.3 — “Polynomial regression is an extension of linear regression” — do you agree with the statement? Support your answer. Also describe why polynomial regression is used.10Topic: Polynomial regression

Yes, I agree. Polynomial regression models y=β0+β1x+β2x2+⋯+βnxn+εy=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\dots+\beta_nx^n+\varepsilony=β0​+β1​x+β2​x2+⋯+βn​xn+ε. Although the curve is non-linear in xxx, the model is linear in its parameters β0,…,βn\beta_0,\dots,\beta_nβ0​,…,βn​. If we define new features x1=x, x2=x2, …, xn=xnx_1=x,\ x_2=x^2,\ \dots,\ x_n=x^nx1​=x, x2​=x2, …, xn​=xn, the model becomes exactly the multiple linear regression y=β0+β1x1+⋯+βnxn+εy=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\dots+\beta_nx_n+\varepsilony=β0​+β1​x1​+⋯+βn​xn​+ε. The design matrix simply gets extra columns:

X=[1x1x12⋯x1n⋮⋮1xmxm2⋯xmn],β^=(XTX)−1XTYX=\begin{bmatrix}1&x_1&x_1^2&\cdots&x_1^n\\\vdots&&&&\vdots\\1&x_m&x_m^2&\cdots&x_m^n\end{bmatrix},\qquad \hat\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^TYX=​1⋮1​x1​xm​​x12​xm2​​⋯⋯​x1n​⋮xmn​​​,β^​=(XTX)−1XTY

So the same least-squares machinery (normal equation, gradient descent, the same assumptions about ε\varepsilonε) is used unchanged. With degree 1, polynomial regression reduces to simple linear regression. It is therefore an extension of linear regression, not a different method.

Why it is used: (1) to capture non-linear trends (curvature) that a straight line cannot fit, e.g. growth curves, a sensor's non-linear calibration, the power–speed relation; (2) it is flexible and can approximate complex smooth functions given enough degree; (3) it is simple and interpretable and still solved by least squares; (4) it reduces underfitting (bias) of a straight-line model. Caution: too high a degree overfits (high variance) and extrapolates badly. Choose the degree by cross-validation and use regularisation.

Source lectureAtia Ma'am · S2 – Linear Regression (MTE 4011 S2_1.pptx, slides 14–15)
2023 · Q1(b)Q2.4 — What do you understand by linear problem and non-linear problem in the context of machine learning? Write down the assumptions of linear regression.10Topic: Linearity · assumptions

Linear problem: the target can be expressed as a linear combination of the input features (y=wTx+by=w^Tx+by=wTx+b), or, for classification, the classes can be separated by a straight line or hyperplane (linearly separable, e.g. AND/OR). Linear models (linear/logistic regression, linear SVM, a single perceptron) solve it. Non-linear problem: the input–output relation is curved, or no single hyperplane can separate the classes (e.g. XOR, concentric circles, image recognition). It needs non-linear models (polynomial features, kernel SVM, decision trees, multilayer neural networks with non-linear activations) or a transformation into a space where it becomes linear.

Assumptions of linear regression: (1) linear relationship between X and Y; (2) independent errors; (3) normally distributed errors for any x; (4) constant error variance (homoscedasticity); (5) hence normally distributed output y about the line; (6) no multicollinearity (features independent of each other).

2023 · Q1(c)Q2.7 — Explain how learning rate impacts the convergence of a model. What potential issues can arise from choosing a learning rate that is too high or too low?08Topic: Learning rate

In gradient descent, θ:=θ−α∇J(θ)\theta:=\theta-\alpha\nabla J(\theta)θ:=θ−α∇J(θ). The learning rate α sets the step size of each update, so it controls both the speed and the stability of convergence (draw Fig. 2.1). With a suitable α the cost decreases every iteration and settles at the minimum.

Too low: tiny steps, very slow convergence and many iterations (high compute cost). Training may stop (iteration limit) before reaching the minimum, and it can get stuck on plateaus or in shallow local minima. Too high: steps overshoot the minimum, so the cost oscillates around it or increases each iteration (divergence). With neural networks this can cause exploding loss (NaN) and never settling. It can also jump out of good minima. Remedies: try values on a log scale while watching the J-vs-iteration curve; use learning-rate decay or schedules and adaptive optimisers (Adam, RMSprop); scale the features.

Source lectureAtia Ma'am · S2 – Linear Regression (MTE 4011 S2_1.pptx, slides 22–24)
2023 · Q1(d)Q2.8 — Explain the difference between batch gradient descent and mini-batch gradient descent.05Topic: GD variants

Batch GD computes the gradient over all mmm training examples for every single update: θ:=θ−αm∑i=1m∇Ji(θ)\theta:=\theta-\frac{\alpha}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\nabla J_i(\theta)θ:=θ−mα​∑i=1m​∇Ji​(θ). This gives exact, smooth updates but only one update per epoch, is slow for large datasets, and needs the whole dataset in memory. Mini-batch GD splits the data into small batches of bbb examples (e.g. 32–256) and updates after each batch: θ:=θ−αb∑i∈B∇Ji(θ)\theta:=\theta-\frac{\alpha}{b}\sum_{i\in B}\nabla J_i(\theta)θ:=θ−bα​∑i∈B​∇Ji​(θ). This gives many updates per epoch and faster, memory-efficient training that is vectorised on GPUs. The noisy gradient gives a slightly fluctuating path, which helps escape shallow local minima. It is the standard choice in deep learning. (See the table in §2.5.2.)

3. Logistic Regression ★★★

3.1 Why Not Linear Regression for Classification?

Linear regression solves regression (a scalar output such as a house price). Logistic regression solves classification, usually binary classification with output 0 or 1 (spam or not, will a customer default on a loan or not). It assigns probabilities to outcomes: the output is the probability that the input belongs to a class. Applying linear regression to classification is a bad idea because:

  1. we want to deal with probabilities, but a line is not a probability;
  2. it is sensitive to outliers: one extreme point changes the model dramatically;
  3. it produces values outside [0, 1], while we need one of two outcomes.

3.2 The Logistic (Sigmoid) Function

Sigmoid / logistic function
p(z)=σ(z)=11+e−z,z=b0+b1x1+⋯+bnxn=xTβp(z)=\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}},\qquad z=b_0+b_1x_1+\dots+b_nx_n=x^T\betap(z)=σ(z)=1+e−z1​,z=b0​+b1​x1​+⋯+bn​xn​=xTβ Properties: range (0, 1), so it can be read as a probability; σ(0)=0.5\sigma(0)=0.5σ(0)=0.5; σ(z)→1\sigma(z)\to1σ(z)→1 as z→+∞z\to+\inftyz→+∞ and →0\to0→0 as z→−∞z\to-\inftyz→−∞; S-shaped, monotonic and differentiable; it saturates, so it is not sensitive to outliers.

p(x)=P(y=1∣x)p(x)=P(y=1\mid x)p(x)=P(y=1∣x), e.g. the probability of default given the credit-card balance. Simple logistic regression has one feature. Multiple (multivariable) logistic regression has many features (balance, age, income …). The lecture calls the latter “multinomial”, though that term usually means more than two classes.

3.2.1 The logit transformation

Solve p=11+e−zp=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}p=1+e−z1​ for zzz:   1+e−z=1p⇒e−z=1−pp⇒z=ln⁡p1−p1+e^{-z}=\dfrac1p\Rightarrow e^{-z}=\dfrac{1-p}{p}\Rightarrow z=\ln\dfrac{p}{1-p}1+e−z=p1​⇒e−z=p1−p​⇒z=ln1−pp​. Hence logit(p)=ln⁡p1−p=b0+b1x1+⋯+bnxn\text{logit}(p)=\ln\frac{p}{1-p}=b_0+b_1x_1+\dots+b_nx_nlogit(p)=ln1−pp​=b0​+b1​x1​+⋯+bn​xn​
[INTUITION]p1−p\frac{p}{1-p}1−pp​ is the odds. Logistic regression is a linear regression on the log-odds, which is why it is a generalised linear model: the logit of the probability, not the probability itself, is linear in the parameters.

The maximum slope is 0.25, at z=0z=0z=0. This compact form is why the sigmoid is convenient for gradient descent and backpropagation.

3.4 Likelihood and Maximum Likelihood Estimation

Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) estimates the parameters of a statistical model by finding the parameter values that maximise the likelihood of the observed data. The aim is the same as in linear regression (optimal bbb values), but here we maximise the (log-)likelihood ℓ(β)=ln⁡L(β)\ell(\beta)=\ln L(\beta)ℓ(β)=lnL(β): β^=arg⁡max⁡β ℓ(β)\hat\beta=\arg\max_\beta\ \ell(\beta)β^​=argmaxβ​ ℓ(β).

Step 1: Probability model of one example. yi∈{0,1}y_i\in\{0,1\}yi​∈{0,1} is a Bernoulli variable with P(yi=1∣xi)=piP(y_i=1\mid x_i)=p_iP(yi​=1∣xi​)=pi​ and P(yi=0∣xi)=1−piP(y_i=0\mid x_i)=1-p_iP(yi​=0∣xi​)=1−pi​, where pi=11+e−xiTβp_i=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x_i^T\beta}}pi​=1+e−xiT​β1​. Both cases in one formula: P(yi∣xi)=pi yi(1−pi)1−yiP(y_i\mid x_i)=p_i^{\,y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}P(yi​∣xi​)=piyi​​(1−pi​)1−yi​
[INTUITION]If yi=1y_i=1yi​=1 the expression is pip_ipi​; if yi=0y_i=0yi​=0 it is 1−pi1-p_i1−pi​. The exponents act as a switch.
Step 2: Likelihood. The nnn observations are independent, so the joint probability is the product: L(β)=∏i=1npi yi(1−pi)1−yiL(\beta)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p_i^{\,y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}L(β)=i=1∏n​piyi​​(1−pi​)1−yi​ This is the likelihood function for logistic regression.
[KEY IDENTITY]Independence: P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).
Step 3: Log-likelihood. The logarithm is monotonic, so maximising LLL is the same as maximising ln⁡L\ln LlnL, and products become sums: ℓ(β)=∑i=1n[yiln⁡pi+(1−yi)ln⁡(1−pi)]\ell(\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[y_i\ln p_i+(1-y_i)\ln(1-p_i)\Big]ℓ(β)=i=1∑n​[yi​lnpi​+(1−yi​)ln(1−pi​)]
[KEY IDENTITY]ln⁡(ab)=ln⁡a+ln⁡b\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln bln(ab)=lna+lnb; ln⁡ak=kln⁡a\ln a^k=k\ln alnak=klna.
Step 4: Simplify using the logit. ln⁡pi−ln⁡(1−pi)=ln⁡pi1−pi=xiTβ\ln p_i-\ln(1-p_i)=\ln\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}=x_i^T\betalnpi​−ln(1−pi​)=ln1−pi​pi​​=xiT​β and 1−pi=11+exiTβ1-p_i=\frac{1}{1+e^{x_i^T\beta}}1−pi​=1+exiT​β1​: ℓ(β)=∑i=1n[yi xiTβ−ln⁡(1+exiTβ)]\ell(\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[y_i\,x_i^T\beta-\ln\big(1+e^{x_i^T\beta}\big)\Big]ℓ(β)=i=1∑n​[yi​xiT​β−ln(1+exiT​β)]
[INTUITION]−ℓ(β)-\ell(\beta)−ℓ(β) is exactly the log-loss / binary cross-entropy cost used in ML libraries.
Step 5: Gradient. Differentiate with respect to βj\beta_jβj​: ∂ℓ∂βj=∑i=1n[yixij−exiTβ1+exiTβxij]=∑i=1n(yi−pi)xij\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta_j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[y_ix_{ij}-\frac{e^{x_i^T\beta}}{1+e^{x_i^T\beta}}x_{ij}\Big]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y_i-p_i\big)x_{ij}∂βj​∂ℓ​=i=1∑n​[yi​xij​−1+exiT​βexiT​β​xij​]=i=1∑n​(yi​−pi​)xij​ In vector form: ∇ℓ(β)=XT(y−p)\nabla\ell(\beta)=X^T(y-p)∇ℓ(β)=XT(y−p).
[KEY IDENTITY]ddβln⁡(1+eu)=eu1+eududβ\frac{d}{d\beta}\ln(1+e^{u})=\frac{e^{u}}{1+e^{u}}\frac{du}{d\beta}dβd​ln(1+eu)=1+eueu​dβdu​ and eu1+eu=σ(u)=p\frac{e^{u}}{1+e^{u}}=\sigma(u)=p1+eueu​=σ(u)=p.
Step 6: Maximum likelihood condition. Set ∇ℓ(β)=0\nabla\ell(\beta)=0∇ℓ(β)=0: ∑i=1n(yi−pi(β^))xij=0,j=0,1,…,n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y_i-p_i(\hat\beta)\big)x_{ij}=0,\quad j=0,1,\dots,ni=1∑n​(yi​−pi​(β^​))xij​=0,j=0,1,…,n Because pip_ipi​ is a non-linear (sigmoid) function of β, there is no closed-form solution. ℓ(β)\ell(\beta)ℓ(β) is concave, so the stationary point is a unique maximum.
[INTUITION]At the optimum the predicted probabilities “balance” the observed labels, feature by feature.
Step 7: Hessian. ∂2ℓ∂βj∂βk=−∑ipi(1−pi)xijxik\dfrac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial\beta_j\partial\beta_k}=-\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)x_{ij}x_{ik}∂βj​∂βk​∂2ℓ​=−∑i​pi​(1−pi​)xij​xik​, i.e. H=−XTWXH=-X^TWXH=−XTWX with W=diag(pi(1−pi))W=\mathrm{diag}\big(p_i(1-p_i)\big)W=diag(pi​(1−pi​)). HHH is negative semi-definite, which confirms concavity.
[KEY IDENTITY]Uses ∂pi/∂βk=pi(1−pi)xik\partial p_i/\partial\beta_k=p_i(1-p_i)x_{ik}∂pi​/∂βk​=pi​(1−pi​)xik​ from §3.3.
Step 8: Iterative solution: Newton–Raphson (lecture) or gradient ascent
β(t+1)=β(t)−H−1(β(t))∇ℓ(β(t))=β(t)+(XTWX)−1XT(y−p)\beta^{(t+1)}=\beta^{(t)}-H^{-1}\big(\beta^{(t)}\big)\nabla\ell\big(\beta^{(t)}\big)=\beta^{(t)}+\big(X^TWX\big)^{-1}X^T\big(y-p\big)β(t+1)=β(t)−H−1(β(t))∇ℓ(β(t))=β(t)+(XTWX)−1XT(y−p) Iterate until the change in β (or in the log-likelihood) is below a threshold. Newton–Raphson converges in a few iterations. This is also called Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS). The simpler alternative is gradient ascent: β:=β+αXT(y−p)\beta:=\beta+\alpha X^T(y-p)β:=β+αXT(y−p).

4. Naïve Bayes Classifier ★★★

4.1 Conditional Probability and Bayes' Theorem

Conditional probability P(A∣B)P(A\mid B)P(A∣B) is the probability of event AAA occurring given that event BBB has occurred: P(A∣B)=P(A∩B)P(B)P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}P(A∣B)=P(B)P(A∩B)​.

Derivation of Bayes' theorem. From the definition, P(A∩B)=P(A∣B)P(B)P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)P(B)P(A∩B)=P(A∣B)P(B) and also P(A∩B)=P(B∣A)P(A)P(A\cap B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)P(A∩B)=P(B∣A)P(A). Equating the two right-hand sides and dividing by P(B)P(B)P(B): P(A∣B)=P(B∣A) P(A)P(B)\boxed{P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}}P(A∣B)=P(B)P(B∣A)P(A)​​
[KEY IDENTITY]P(A∩B)=P(B∩A)P(A\cap B)=P(B\cap A)P(A∩B)=P(B∩A): intersection is symmetric.
TermNameMeaning in classification (AAA = class CkC_kCk​, BBB = features xxx)
P(A)P(A)P(A)PriorHow common the class is before seeing the features
P(B∣A)P(B\mid A)P(B∣A)LikelihoodHow probable these features are if the class is CkC_kCk​
P(B)P(B)P(B)EvidenceTotal probability of the features (the same for all classes)
P(A∣B)P(A\mid B)P(A∣B)PosteriorProbability of the class after seeing the features

4.2 From Bayes to Naïve Bayes

Step 1. Goal: find the posterior P(Ck∣x)P(C_k\mid x)P(Ck​∣x) for features x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)x=(x1​,…,xn​): P(Ck∣x)=P(x∣Ck) P(Ck)P(x)P(C_k\mid x)=\frac{P(x\mid C_k)\,P(C_k)}{P(x)}P(Ck​∣x)=P(x)P(x∣Ck​)P(Ck​)​
[INTUITION]Estimating the joint P(x1,…,xn∣Ck)P(x_1,\dots,x_n\mid C_k)P(x1​,…,xn​∣Ck​) directly needs a huge amount of data: every combination of feature values.
Step 2: The naïve assumption. The features are conditionally independent given the class: P(x1,x2,…,xn∣Ck)=P(x1∣Ck) P(x2∣Ck)⋯P(xn∣Ck)=∏i=1nP(xi∣Ck)P(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n\mid C_k)=P(x_1\mid C_k)\,P(x_2\mid C_k)\cdots P(x_n\mid C_k)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}P(x_i\mid C_k)P(x1​,x2​,…,xn​∣Ck​)=P(x1​∣Ck​)P(x2​∣Ck​)⋯P(xn​∣Ck​)=i=1∏n​P(xi​∣Ck​)
[KEY IDENTITY]For independent events, the joint probability is the product of the individual probabilities.
Step 3. Substitute: P(Ck∣x1,…,xn)=P(Ck)∏i=1nP(xi∣Ck)P(x1,…,xn)P(C_k\mid x_1,\dots,x_n)=\frac{P(C_k)\prod_{i=1}^{n}P(x_i\mid C_k)}{P(x_1,\dots,x_n)}P(Ck​∣x1​,…,xn​)=P(x1​,…,xn​)P(Ck​)∏i=1n​P(xi​∣Ck​)​
[INTUITION]P(x)P(x)P(x) is the same for every class, so it is a normalising constant.
Step 4: Naïve Bayes classifier formula (lecture)
P(Ck∣x)∝P(Ck)∏i=1nP(xi∣Ck)⟹C=arg⁡max⁡Ck P(Ck)∏i=1nP(xi∣Ck)P(C_k\mid x)\propto P(C_k)\prod_{i=1}^{n}P(x_i\mid C_k)\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad C=\arg\max_{C_k}\ P(C_k)\prod_{i=1}^{n}P(x_i\mid C_k)P(Ck​∣x)∝P(Ck​)i=1∏n​P(xi​∣Ck​)⟹C=argCk​max​ P(Ck​)i=1∏n​P(xi​∣Ck​) Choose the class with the highest (unnormalised) posterior. To get actual probabilities, divide each score by the sum of all class scores.

4.2.1 Why “naïve”?

The naïve assumption is that each feature is independent of the others given the class. Example: a fruit is an apple if it is red, round and about 8 cm in diameter. Naïve Bayes treats each of these features as contributing independently to the probability that the fruit is an apple, and ignores any correlation between colour, roundness and diameter. In reality features are usually correlated, so the assumption is “naïve”. Even so, the classifier works surprisingly well.

4.2.2 Advantages and disadvantages

Advantages
  • Simple to understand and implement
  • Very fast to train and predict
  • Works well even with small training data
  • Scales well to high dimensions (many features)
  • Not sensitive to irrelevant features
  • Competitive with SVM and random forests, especially for text
Disadvantages
  • The independence assumption is usually not true
  • Zero-frequency problem: an unseen feature value makes the whole product 0 (fixed by Laplace smoothing)
  • Probability estimates are poorly calibrated
  • Continuous features need a distribution assumption (Gaussian NB)

Why it is so powerful for text classification: it matches the bag-of-words assumptions: (1) the occurrence of any word given the label is independent of other words; (2) a word's occurrence is independent of its position in the document. For text, a document is treated as a bunch of words thrown together.

4.2.3 Laplace (add-one) smoothing

P(xi=v∣Ck)=count(xi=v, Ck)+1count(Ck)+∣Vi∣P(x_i=v\mid C_k)=\frac{\text{count}(x_i=v,\ C_k)+1}{\text{count}(C_k)+|V_i|}P(xi​=v∣Ck​)=count(Ck​)+∣Vi​∣count(xi​=v, Ck​)+1​

where ∣Vi∣|V_i|∣Vi​∣ is the number of distinct values of feature iii. No probability is ever exactly 0.

2023 · Q2(b)Q4.1 — What is Bayes theorem? Shortly describe Naïve Bayes classifier.10Topic: Bayes theorem · NB

Bayes' theorem relates the reverse conditional probabilities P(A∣B)P(A\mid B)P(A∣B) and P(B∣A)P(B\mid A)P(B∣A): P(A∣B)=P(B∣A)P(A)P(B)P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}P(A∣B)=P(B)P(B∣A)P(A)​, where P(A)P(A)P(A) is the prior, P(B∣A)P(B\mid A)P(B∣A) the likelihood, P(B)P(B)P(B) the evidence and P(A∣B)P(A\mid B)P(A∣B) the posterior. (Show the two-line derivation of §4.1.) It updates our belief about AAA after observing BBB.

Naïve Bayes classifier: an efficient supervised, probability-based classification algorithm. To classify features x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)x=(x1​,…,xn​) it computes the posterior of each class with Bayes' theorem. It makes the naïve assumption that the features are conditionally independent given the class, so P(x∣Ck)=∏iP(xi∣Ck)P(x\mid C_k)=\prod_iP(x_i\mid C_k)P(x∣Ck​)=∏i​P(xi​∣Ck​). The evidence P(x)P(x)P(x) is the same for all classes and is dropped. The predicted class is C=arg⁡max⁡CkP(Ck)∏i=1nP(xi∣Ck)C=\arg\max_{C_k}P(C_k)\prod_{i=1}^{n}P(x_i\mid C_k)C=argCk​max​P(Ck​)i=1∏n​P(xi​∣Ck​)

Training is just counting: the priors are class frequencies, and the likelihoods are per-feature frequencies within each class (Gaussian for continuous features, with Laplace smoothing to avoid zeros). Advantages: simple, fast, works on small data, scales to many features, strong for text/spam filtering. Disadvantage: the independence assumption is rarely true, and there is a zero-frequency problem.

5. Generalisation, Bias–Variance and Regularisation ★★★

5.1 Generalisation, Overfitting and Underfitting

In supervised learning we build a model on the training data and want it to make accurate predictions on new, unseen data with the same characteristics. If it does, the model generalises from the training set to the test set. The goal is a model that generalises as accurately as possible.

AspectUnderfittingOverfitting
DefinitionThe model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern of the dataThe model is too complex and learns the underlying pattern and the noise in the training data
Training errorHighVery low
Test errorHighHigh (poor generalisation)
Bias / varianceHigh bias, low varianceLow bias, high variance
ExampleA linear model fitted to highly non-linear dataA deep decision tree memorising the training data; a degree-15 polynomial on 10 points
CausesToo few parameters, insufficient training, too strong regularisationToo many parameters, no regularisation, too little training data
SolutionsIncrease model complexity, reduce regularisation, add relevant features, train longerSimplify the model, regularise, cross-validate, gather more data, prune trees, early stopping, dropout

Model complexity vs dataset size: the more varied the data points, the more complex a model can be used without overfitting. Collecting more data usually gives more variety, so larger datasets allow more complex models. However, simply duplicating the same points or collecting very similar data does not help.

5.2 The Bias–Variance Trade-off

We want a model that (1) captures the relationships in the training data and (2) generalises well to unseen data. It is generally impossible to achieve both perfectly at the same time. This is the bias–variance trade-off.

  • Bias: error from wrong or overly simple assumptions in the learning algorithm. High bias: the algorithm misses the relevant relationships between features and target, i.e. underfitting.
  • Variance: error from sensitivity to small changes in the training set. High variance: the algorithm models the noise, i.e. overfitting.
Decomposition of the expected test error (squared loss)
E[(y−f^(x))2]=(E[f^(x)]−f(x))2⏟Bias2+E[(f^(x)−E[f^(x)])2]⏟Variance+σ2⏟irreducible noiseE\big[(y-\hat f(x))^2\big]=\underbrace{\big(E[\hat f(x)]-f(x)\big)^2}_{\text{Bias}^2}+\underbrace{E\big[(\hat f(x)-E[\hat f(x)])^2\big]}_{\text{Variance}}+\underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible noise}}E[(y−f^​(x))2]=Bias2(E[f^​(x)]−f(x))2​​+VarianceE[(f^​(x)−E[f^​(x)])2]​​+irreducible noiseσ2​​
[INTUITION]As complexity grows, bias falls but variance rises. Total error is U-shaped, and the best model sits at the bottom of the U. Low bias with high variance, or low variance with high bias: we cannot minimise both at once.

Dartboard picture: low bias + low variance = shots tight around the bull's-eye (ideal); high bias + low variance = tight group but off-centre (underfit); low bias + high variance = centred on average but scattered (overfit); high bias + high variance = scattered and off-centre.

5.3 Regularisation

Definition
Regularisation adds a penalty on the size of the model parameters to the cost function, which discourages overly complex models: Jreg(θ)=12m∑i=1m(hθ(xi)−yi)2⏟data fit+λ2m∑j=1nθj2⏟penaltyJ_{reg}(\theta)=\underbrace{\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\big(h_\theta(x_i)-y_i\big)^2}_{\text{data fit}}+\underbrace{\frac{\lambda}{2m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\theta_j^2}_{\text{penalty}}Jreg​(θ)=data fit2m1​i=1∑m​(hθ​(xi​)−yi​)2​​+penalty2mλ​j=1∑n​θj2​​​ λ (regularisation parameter) controls the trade-off: λ = 0 gives no regularisation (risk of overfitting); very large λ forces all θj→0\theta_j\to0θj​→0 (underfitting). θ0\theta_0θ0​ is not penalised.
TypePenaltyEffect
L2 / Ridgeλ∑θj2\lambda\sum\theta_j^2λ∑θj2​Shrinks all weights smoothly toward 0. Keeps all features. Makes XTX+λIX^TX+\lambda IXTX+λI invertible.
L1 / Lassoλ∑∣θj∣\lambda\sum|\theta_j|λ∑∣θj​∣Drives some weights to exactly 0, so it also does automatic feature selection.
Elastic Netλ1∑∣θj∣+λ2∑θj2\lambda_1\sum|\theta_j|+\lambda_2\sum\theta_j^2λ1​∑∣θj​∣+λ2​∑θj2​A combination of both.
Other formsDropout, early stopping, pruning (trees), soft margin C (SVM)Limit effective model complexity.

How it prevents overfitting: (1) Small parameter values give a simpler, smoother hypothesis. For example, the large high-order polynomial coefficients that make wiggly curves are suppressed. (2) The model cannot fit every noisy point, so variance is reduced at the cost of a little bias, which moves it toward the sweet spot of the bias–variance curve. (3) It keeps all features but lets each contribute a little, which works well when there are many features each contributing a bit to predicting yyy. (4) The gradient-descent update becomes θj:=θj(1−αλm)−α1m∑i(hθ(xi)−yi)xj,i\theta_j:=\theta_j\big(1-\alpha\frac{\lambda}{m}\big)-\alpha\frac{1}{m}\sum_i(h_\theta(x_i)-y_i)x_{j,i}θj​:=θj​(1−αmλ​)−αm1​∑i​(hθ​(xi​)−yi​)xj,i​: each step shrinks the weights (weight decay). (5) It fixes the non-invertibility of XTXX^TXXTX.

5.4 Covariance and Correlation (for PCA)

Definitions

5.5 Solved Past Questions

2024 · Q2(c)Q5.1 — Define overfitting and underfitting. Also, describe bias-variance trade-off.10Topic: Generalisation

Overfitting: the model is too complex and learns not only the underlying pattern but also the noise in the training data. It performs very well on the training set but poorly on unseen test data (e.g. a deep decision tree memorising the data). It is caused by too many parameters, lack of regularisation or insufficient data.

Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern, so it performs poorly on both training and test sets (e.g. a straight line fitted to highly non-linear data). It is caused by too few parameters, insufficient training or too strong regularisation. Draw Fig. 5.1.

Bias–variance trade-off: we want a model that captures the relationships in the training data and also generalises to unseen data, but generally we cannot achieve both at once. Bias is the error from overly simple or wrong assumptions; high bias means relevant relations are missed (underfitting). Variance is the error from sensitivity to small changes in the training set; high variance means the noise is modelled (overfitting). Increasing model complexity lowers bias but raises variance. Expected error = Bias² + Variance + irreducible noise, so total error is U-shaped against complexity (draw the §5.2 curve). The best model balances the two at the minimum of total error (low bias → high variance, low variance → high bias). Tools to manage it: cross-validation, regularisation, more data, pruning, bagging (reduces variance).

Source lectureAtia Ma'am · S4 – Generalisation & Decision Trees (MTE 4011 S4.pdf, pp. 1–4)
2022 · Q3(b)Q5.2 — What do you mean by Overfitting and underfitting? Write down a way to minimize both of the issues.08Topic: Generalisation

Define both as in Q5.1 (with Fig. 5.1). A way to minimise both: choose the right model complexity with cross-validation, together with regularisation. Split the data (k-fold cross-validation). Train models of increasing complexity (e.g. polynomial degree, tree depth) or with different regularisation strengths λ. Plot training and validation error, and pick the model where validation error is minimum. Left of that point both errors are high (underfitting: increase complexity, reduce λ, add features). Right of it the training error is low but validation error rises (overfitting: add λ, simplify or prune, get more data, stop early). This finds the sweet spot of the bias–variance trade-off, so both problems are minimised at once.

Source lectureAtia Ma'am · S4 – Generalisation & Decision Trees (MTE 4011 S4.pdf, pp. 1–2)
2023 · Q3(c)Q5.3 — What is meant by regularization in machine learning? How does it help in prevent overfitting?10Topic: Regularisation

Regularisation is a technique that adds a penalty on the size of the model's parameters to the cost function, which keeps the model simple: Jreg(θ)=12m∑i(hθ(xi)−yi)2+λ2m∑j=1nθj2J_{reg}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2m}\sum_i(h_\theta(x_i)-y_i)^2+\frac{\lambda}{2m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\theta_j^2Jreg​(θ)=2m1​∑i​(hθ​(xi​)−yi​)2+2mλ​∑j=1n​θj2​. λ controls the strength. Types: L2/Ridge (∑θj2\sum\theta_j^2∑θj2​), L1/Lasso (∑∣θj∣\sum|\theta_j|∑∣θj​∣, which also selects features), Elastic Net; and in other models dropout, early stopping, tree pruning and the SVM C parameter.

How it prevents overfitting: write points (1)–(5) of §5.3: small weights give a simpler, smoother hypothesis; noise cannot be fitted, so variance falls in exchange for a little bias; all features are kept but each contributes a little; weight decay in the gradient update; and the normal equation becomes (XTX+λL)−1XTY(X^TX+\lambda L)^{-1}X^TY(XTX+λL)−1XTY, which is always invertible. Choose λ by cross-validation: λ too large causes underfitting.

Source lectureAtia Ma'am · S2 – Linear Regression (MTE 4011 S2_1.pptx, slide 21); S4 – Generalisation & Decision Trees (MTE 4011 S4.pdf, pp. 1–2) — Penalty formulas (L1/L2, λ) not in slides
2023 · Q2(c)Q5.4 — Write short notes on (i) Covariance and (ii) Correlation. Why is it necessary to compute a covariance matrix for principle component analysis?10Topic: Covariance · PCA

(i) Covariance measures how two variables vary together: cov(X,Y)=1n−1∑i(xi−xˉ)(yi−yˉ)\mathrm{cov}(X,Y)=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)cov(X,Y)=n−11​∑i​(xi​−xˉ)(yi​−yˉ​). Positive means they increase together, negative means one increases as the other decreases, and zero means no linear relationship. Its magnitude depends on units, so it shows direction but not strength.

(ii) Correlation is covariance standardised by the standard deviations: r=cov(X,Y)σXσYr=\dfrac{\mathrm{cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}r=σX​σY​cov(X,Y)​, with −1≤r≤1-1\le r\le1−1≤r≤1. It is dimensionless and gives both the direction and the strength of the linear relationship (±1 perfect, 0 none). Include the worked example of §5.4.

Why PCA needs the covariance matrix: (1) PCA looks for new orthogonal axes (principal components) along which the data varies the most. Variance and the linear relationships between features are exactly what the covariance matrix Σ\SigmaΣ contains: variances on the diagonal and covariances off the diagonal. (2) The principal components are the eigenvectors of Σ, and the eigenvalues give the variance captured by each component: Σv=λv\Sigma v=\lambda vΣv=λv. So computing Σ is the essential step. (3) Large off-diagonal covariances show redundant, correlated features. PCA removes this redundancy by rotating to uncorrelated components (Σ becomes diagonal in the new basis). (4) Sorting eigenvalues tells us how many components to keep for a given percentage of total variance, which is how dimensionality is reduced. (If the features have different units, the correlation matrix, i.e. the covariance of standardised data, is used.)

Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §5.4 of this book)

6. Decision Trees ★★★

6.1 What is a Decision Tree?

A decision tree is a supervised model for classification and regression in the form of a tree structure. It predicts the target by learning simple if–then decision rules from the data features. An instance is classified by starting at the root and moving down branches, according to its feature values, until a leaf is reached.

TermMeaning
Root nodeThe starting point. It contains the complete dataset and splits on the attribute that best separates the data.
Decision (internal) nodeAny node other than the root or a leaf, where the data is split further by a rule on a feature.
Leaf (terminal) nodeA node at the bottom that does not split further. It holds the class or value.
Branch / pathThe sequence of nodes and branches from the root down to a leaf, i.e. one decision rule.

The key questions are: which attribute to start with (the root)? Which to use next? When to stop? Key requirements: attribute–value description of the data, predefined classes, and sufficient data. Split criteria: (1) the Gini index (CART), (2) information entropy / gain (ID3, C4.5), (3) variance reduction (regression trees).

6.2 Entropy and Information Gain (ID3)

Formulas
Shannon entropy of a set SSS with class proportions pip_ipi​: E(S)=H(S)=−∑i=1cpilog⁡2pi\displaystyle E(S)=H(S)=-\sum_{i=1}^{c}p_i\log_2p_iE(S)=H(S)=−i=1∑c​pi​log2​pi​
Weighted entropy after splitting on attribute XXX: E(T,X)=∑v∈values(X)P(v) E(Tv)=∑v∣Tv∣∣T∣E(Tv)\displaystyle E(T,X)=\sum_{v\in \text{values}(X)}P(v)\,E(T_v)=\sum_v\frac{|T_v|}{|T|}E(T_v)E(T,X)=v∈values(X)∑​P(v)E(Tv​)=v∑​∣T∣∣Tv​∣​E(Tv​)
Information gain: IG(T,X)=E(T)−E(T,X)\displaystyle IG(T,X)=E(T)-E(T,X)IG(T,X)=E(T)−E(T,X) = entropy(parent) − weighted average entropy(children)
  • Entropy measures the impurity or unpredictability of a set. A completely homogeneous set (all one class) has entropy 0. An equally divided binary set has entropy 1.
  • ID3 is a top-down, greedy search. At each node it picks the attribute with the highest information gain (largest impurity reduction). The root has the maximum IG. A branch with entropy greater than 0 needs further splitting, and leaves have entropy 0.
  • Useful values: H(9,5)=0.940H(9,5)=0.940H(9,5)=0.940, H(3,1)=0.811H(3,1)=0.811H(3,1)=0.811, H(2,1)=0.918H(2,1)=0.918H(2,1)=0.918, H(2,3)=0.971H(2,3)=0.971H(2,3)=0.971, H(1,1)=1H(1,1)=1H(1,1)=1, H(k,0)=0H(k,0)=0H(k,0)=0.

6.3 Gini Index (CART)

Gini index and impurity reduction
G(X)=1−∑ipi2\displaystyle G(X)=1-\sum_i p_i^2G(X)=1−i∑​pi2​   (0 = pure; maximum 0.5 for two balanced classes)

CART uses the Gini index. It gives almost the same splits as entropy, but it avoids logarithms, so it is computationally cheaper and often preferred.

6.4 Advantages and Disadvantages of Decision Trees

Advantages
  • Simple to understand, interpret and visualise (white-box rules)
  • Little data preparation; no normalisation needed
  • Handles both numerical and categorical data
  • Can be used for classification and regression
  • Non-linear relationships do not affect performance
  • Fast prediction; implicit feature selection
  • Flexible: can be modified to make the tree balanced and practical
Disadvantages
  • Overfitting: the tree captures noise in the data
  • High variance / unstable: small variation in the data can change the tree a lot
  • A very complex tree has low bias but struggles with new data
  • Greedy splits are not globally optimal
  • Biased toward attributes with many levels (information gain)
  • Usually less accurate than the best methods (SVM, ensembles)

6.5 Pruning

Definition
Pruning reduces the size of a decision tree by removing branches (sub-trees) that have little predictive power and replacing them with leaves. The result is a smaller tree with fewer splits: a better predictor at the cost of a little extra bias. Decision trees tend to overfit because every split is optimised for the training data, so they rarely generalise well to other data.
  • Pre-pruning (early stopping): stop growing while building, using a maximum depth, a minimum number of samples to split or per leaf, a minimum information gain, or a statistical significance test.
  • Post-pruning (better): grow a large tree, then prune it back to a smaller sub-tree:
    • Reduced-error pruning: replace a sub-tree with a leaf if the validation accuracy does not drop.
    • Cost-complexity (“weakest-link”) pruning (CART): minimise Rα(T)=R(T)+α∣T∣R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha|T|Rα​(T)=R(T)+α∣T∣, where R(T)R(T)R(T) is the training error and ∣T∣|T|∣T∣ the number of leaves. Increasing α repeatedly removes the weakest link (the sub-tree with the smallest error increase per removed leaf). The best α is chosen by cross-validation.
Advantages of pruningDisadvantages of pruning
  • Reduces overfitting and improves accuracy on unseen data
  • Smaller, simpler, more interpretable tree
  • Faster prediction and less memory
  • Reduces variance (more stable model)
  • Removes branches built on noise or outliers
  • Adds a little bias; may remove useful branches (risk of underfitting)
  • Post-pruning is extra computation (grow the full tree, then evaluate sub-trees)
  • Needs a validation set or cross-validation, which means less training data
  • Pre-pruning can stop too early (the “horizon effect”)
  • Hyper-parameters (depth, α) must be tuned

6.6 Bagging and Random Forest

Weak learners: a weak learner is only slightly better than a coin flip (e.g. a depth-1 tree), but combining many weak learners can give an extremely powerful classifier (“wisdom of the crowd”). Averaging a set of observations reduces variance. Ideally we would build one tree on each of many training sets, but we have only one dataset.

Bagging (bootstrap aggregation): draw repeated bootstrap samples (with replacement) from the single dataset, grow a fully grown, unpruned tree on each, and aggregate: average for regression and majority vote for classification. Pruning reduces variance but adds bias; bagging reduces variance without extra bias. Problem: the bagged trees are highly correlated. Every dataset has a strong predictor, so all trees make the same top splits and look similar. Random forest fixes this by considering only a random subset of features (≈p\approx\sqrt{p}≈p​) at each split, which decorrelates the trees.

2024 · Q3(c)Q6.2 — Define pruning. What are the advantages and disadvantages of it.08Topic: Pruning

Pruning is the process of reducing the size of a decision tree by removing sub-trees (branches) that add little predictive power and replacing them with leaf nodes. It gives a smaller tree with fewer splits, trading a little extra bias for a large reduction in variance. There are two kinds: pre-pruning (stop growth early using max depth, min samples, min gain) and post-pruning (grow a large tree, then cut it back: reduced-error pruning or cost-complexity “weakest-link” pruning, Rα(T)=R(T)+α∣T∣R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha|T|Rα​(T)=R(T)+α∣T∣). Then write the advantages/disadvantages table of §6.5.

Source lectureAtia Ma'am · S4 – Generalisation & Decision Trees (MTE 4011 S4.pdf, pp. 29–31) — Pros/cons of pruning only implied (bias vs variance)
2023 · Q4(b)Q6.3 — Explain how pruning can be used to prevent overfitting in decision trees.10Topic: Pruning

Why trees overfit: a tree keeps splitting until the leaves are pure, and every split is optimised for the training set. Deep branches end up modelling noise and outliers (tiny leaves with one or two samples). The tree becomes low-bias but high-variance: perfect training accuracy, poor test accuracy, and unstable if the data changes slightly.

How pruning prevents it:

  1. Pre-pruning stops the growth before the tree fits noise: limit the maximum depth, require a minimum number of samples to split or per leaf, require a minimum information-gain or Gini reduction, or use a χ² significance test.
  2. Post-pruning (preferred): grow the full tree, then remove branches from the bottom up.
    • Reduced-error pruning: for each internal node, replace its sub-tree with a leaf holding the majority class. Keep the change if the error on a separate validation set does not increase.
    • Cost-complexity (weakest-link) pruning: minimise Rα(T)=R(T)+α∣T∣R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha|T|Rα​(T)=R(T)+α∣T∣. The penalty on the number of leaves makes each extra branch “pay” for itself with a real error reduction. Increasing α gives a sequence of smaller sub-trees, and the best α is chosen by cross-validation.
  3. Effect: branches that only fitted noise are removed, so the tree captures the general pattern. Variance falls a great deal and bias rises only a little, which lowers the test error (bias–variance trade-off). Draw a before/after sketch of a deep tree cut back to a shallow one.
  4. Alternative variance reduction: ensembles (bagging, random forests) of unpruned trees.
Source lectureAtia Ma'am · S4 – Generalisation & Decision Trees (MTE 4011 S4.pdf, pp. 29–31)
2022 · Q4(d)Q6.4 — What are the advantages and disadvantages of using decision trees as a machine learning model?05Topic: Decision trees

Write the two lists of §6.4. Advantages: easy to understand, interpret and visualise; little data preparation (no scaling); handles numerical and categorical data; classification and regression; captures non-linear relations; fast. Disadvantages: prone to overfitting; high variance and instability (small data changes alter the tree); greedy, locally optimal splits; bias toward many-valued attributes; usually less accurate than SVMs and ensembles.

Source lectureAtia Ma'am · S4 – Generalisation & Decision Trees (MTE 4011 S4.pdf, pp. 8–9); S4 – Generalisation & Decision Trees (MTE 4011 S4.pdf, p. 29)

7. Support Vector Machines (SVM) ★★★

7.1 Idea: the Maximum-Margin Hyperplane

SVM is a very popular supervised classification algorithm (also usable for regression). It finds a hyperplane (a flat boundary) that separates the classes with the maximum margin, i.e. the largest distance to the nearest training point of any class. In general, the larger the margin, the lower the generalisation error. The points closest to the boundary are the support vectors. They store all the information about the decision boundary: moving other points changes nothing, but moving a support vector changes the model. Each class has at least one support vector, and the hyperplane can be rebuilt from the support vectors alone, so the model is memory-friendly even with a huge number of features.

7.2 Hyperplane and Classification Rule

In geometry a hyperplane is a subspace with one dimension fewer than its ambient space. It splits the space into two parts. General equation: wTx+b=0w^Tx+b=0wTx+b=0 (in 2-D a line, in 3-D a plane). Lecture example: x2=−x1+5⇒x1+x2−5=0x_2=-x_1+5\Rightarrow x_1+x_2-5=0x2​=−x1​+5⇒x1​+x2​−5=0, i.e. w=(1,1)T, b=−5w=(1,1)^T,\ b=-5w=(1,1)T, b=−5. Point (1, 1): 1+1−5=−3<01+1-5=-3<01+1−5=−3<0 → negative side. Point (10, 10): 10+10−5=15>010+10-5=15>010+10−5=15>0 → positive side. So the sign of wTx+bw^Tx+bwTx+b gives the class.

Canonical constraints. Require wTxi+b≥+δw^Tx_i+b\ge+\deltawTxi​+b≥+δ for yi=+1y_i=+1yi​=+1 and ≤−δ\le-\delta≤−δ for yi=−1y_i=-1yi​=−1. Scaling w,bw,bw,b lets us set δ=1\delta=1δ=1 (for mathematical convenience). Then both cases combine into one constraint: yi (wTxi+b)≥1,i=1,…,Ny_i\,(w^Tx_i+b)\ge1,\qquad i=1,\dots,Nyi​(wTxi​+b)≥1,i=1,…,N Support vectors are the points where equality holds: yi(wTxi+b)=1y_i(w^Tx_i+b)=1yi​(wTxi​+b)=1, i.e. on H1H_1H1​ or H2H_2H2​.
[INTUITION]Multiplying by yi=±1y_i=\pm1yi​=±1 flips the inequality for the negative class, so one expression covers both.

7.3 Margin Width and the Primal Problem

Step 1. The distance from a point x0x_0x0​ to the hyperplane wTx+b=0w^Tx+b=0wTx+b=0 is d=∣wTx0+b∣∥w∥d=\dfrac{|w^Tx_0+b|}{\lVert w\rVert}d=∥w∥∣wTx0​+b∣​.
[KEY IDENTITY]Point-to-plane distance; www is the normal vector of the plane.
Step 2. For a support vector ∣wTxs+b∣=1|w^Tx_s+b|=1∣wTxs​+b∣=1, so the distance from H to H₁ (and to H₂) is 1∥w∥\dfrac{1}{\lVert w\rVert}∥w∥1​.
Step 3. Total margin between H₁ and H₂: 2∥w∥\dfrac{2}{\lVert w\rVert}∥w∥2​. We want to maximise it.
Step 4. Maximising 2∥w∥\frac{2}{\lVert w\rVert}∥w∥2​ is equivalent to minimising ∥w∥\lVert w\rVert∥w∥, and hence to minimising 12∥w∥2\frac12\lVert w\rVert^221​∥w∥2 (smooth and convex): Primal (hard margin):min⁡w,b 12∥w∥2s.t.yi(wTxi+b)≥1, i=1,…,N\textbf{Primal (hard margin):}\quad \min_{w,b}\ \frac12\lVert w\rVert^2\quad\text{s.t.}\quad y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\ge1,\ i=1,\dots,NPrimal (hard margin):w,bmin​ 21​∥w∥2s.t.yi​(wTxi​+b)≥1, i=1,…,N
[INTUITION]Squaring removes the square root in ∥w∥\lVert w\rVert∥w∥ and makes the objective a convex quadratic (a QP with one global optimum). The ½ tidies the derivative.

7.5 Soft-Margin SVM (Non-Separable Data)

Real-world data is rarely linearly separable: there is noise, outliers and overlap. A hard-margin SVM insists on perfect separation with the widest margin, which is impossible or very fragile with noise. A soft-margin SVM allows some margin violations or misclassifications using slack variables ξi≥0\xi_i\ge0ξi​≥0 (the distance by which point iii violates its margin), and penalises them with a cost parameter CCC:

min⁡w,b,ξ 12∥w∥2+C∑i=1nξi ks.t.yi(wTxi+b)≥1−ξi,  ξi≥0\min_{w,b,\xi}\ \frac12\lVert w\rVert^2+C\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_i^{\,k}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\ge1-\xi_i,\ \ \xi_i\ge0w,b,ξmin​ 21​∥w∥2+Ci=1∑n​ξik​s.t.yi​(wTxi​+b)≥1−ξi​,  ξi​≥0
  • ξi=0\xi_i=0ξi​=0: correctly classified outside the margin. 0<ξi≤10<\xi_i\le10<ξi​≤1: inside the margin but correct. ξi>1\xi_i>1ξi​>1: misclassified.
  • k=1k=1k=1: hinge loss. k=2k=2k=2: quadratic loss. The hinge loss equivalent is min⁡ 12∥w∥2+C∑imax⁡(0, 1−yi(wTxi+b))\min\ \frac12\lVert w\rVert^2+C\sum_i\max\big(0,\,1-y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\big)min 21​∥w∥2+C∑i​max(0,1−yi​(wTxi​+b)).
  • C large: violations are heavily penalised, so the algorithm tries for 100 % separation (narrow margin, risk of overfitting). C small: a wider margin is allowed with more misclassified points (more regularisation).

7.7 The Kernel Trick

Many real problems are non-linear. SVM can map the data into a higher-dimensional space with a feature map ϕ(x)\phi(x)ϕ(x) in which it becomes linearly separable. Lecture example: points described by (latitude x1x_1x1​, longitude x2x_2x2​), with one class forming a ring around the other, are not linearly separable in 2-D. Adding the feature “altitude” x12+x22x_1^2+x_2^2x12​+x22​ makes them separable by a plane. SVM learns concepts (features) that were not explicitly measured in the original dataset. Transforming every point explicitly is expensive in computation and memory. However, the dual uses the data only through dot products xiTxjx_i^Tx_jxiT​xj​, so we replace them by a kernel K(xi,xj)=ϕ(xi)Tϕ(xj)K(x_i,x_j)=\phi(x_i)^T\phi(x_j)K(xi​,xj​)=ϕ(xi​)Tϕ(xj​) that computes the high-dimensional dot product without ever computing ϕ(x)\phi(x)ϕ(x). This is the kernel trick.

Example (lecture): K(x,z)=(xTz)2K(x,z)=(x^Tz)^2K(x,z)=(xTz)2 is a valid kernel. K(x,z)=(∑ixizi)(∑jxjzj)=∑i∑jxixjzizj=∑i,j(xixj)(zizj)=ϕ(x)Tϕ(z)K(x,z)=\Big(\sum_ix_iz_i\Big)\Big(\sum_jx_jz_j\Big)=\sum_i\sum_jx_ix_jz_iz_j=\sum_{i,j}(x_ix_j)(z_iz_j)=\phi(x)^T\phi(z)K(x,z)=(i∑​xi​zi​)(j∑​xj​zj​)=i∑​j∑​xi​xj​zi​zj​=i,j∑​(xi​xj​)(zi​zj​)=ϕ(x)Tϕ(z) with ϕ(x)=(xixj)i,j=1..n\phi(x)=(x_ix_j)_{i,j=1..n}ϕ(x)=(xi​xj​)i,j=1..n​ (all pairwise products, n2n^2n2 features). Computing KKK costs O(n)O(n)O(n) instead of O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2).
[INTUITION]The data is never sent into the high-dimensional space, yet we get all the benefits: this is the “kernel trick”.
Kernel definition and Mercer's condition
A kernel function corresponds to a dot product of two feature vectors in some expanded feature space. It defines inner products, and therefore similarity, in the transformed space. Not every similarity measure is a valid kernel. Mercer's condition: KKK is a valid kernel (it can be written as ϕ(x)Tϕ(z)\phi(x)^T\phi(z)ϕ(x)Tϕ(z)) if and only if it is symmetric, K(x,z)=K(z,x)K(x,z)=K(z,x)K(x,z)=K(z,x), and positive semi-definite: ∑i∑jcicj K(xi,xj)≥0for all x1..xn and all real constants c1..cn\sum_{i}\sum_{j}c_ic_j\,K(x_i,x_j)\ge0\quad\text{for all } x_1..x_n \text{ and all real constants } c_1..c_ni∑​j∑​ci​cj​K(xi​,xj​)≥0for all x1​..xn​ and all real constants c1​..cn​ Equivalently, every Gram matrix [K(xi,xj)][K(x_i,x_j)][K(xi​,xj​)] is positive semi-definite (continuous form: ∬K(x,z)g(x)g(z) dx dz≥0\iint K(x,z)g(x)g(z)\,dx\,dz\ge0∬K(x,z)g(x)g(z)dxdz≥0 for all square-integrable ggg). This guarantees a convex dual with a unique optimum.
KernelFormulaUse
LinearK(xi,xj)=xiTxjK(x_i,x_j)=x_i^Tx_jK(xi​,xj​)=xiT​xj​No transformation; linearly separable or high-dimensional data (text)
Polynomial (homogeneous / inhomogeneous)(xiTxj)d(x_i^Tx_j)^d(xiT​xj​)d  /  (xiTxj+1)d(x_i^Tx_j+1)^d(xiT​xj​+1)dFeature interactions up to degree d (image processing)
Gaussian RBFexp⁡ ⁣(−∥xi−xj∥22σ2)\exp\!\Big(-\dfrac{\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)exp(−2σ2∥xi​−xj​∥2​)General-purpose non-linear kernel; infinite-dimensional feature space
Laplace RBFexp⁡ ⁣(−∥xi−xj∥σ)\exp\!\Big(-\dfrac{\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert}{\sigma}\Big)exp(−σ∥xi​−xj​∥​)General purpose, when there is no prior knowledge
Hyperbolic tangent / sigmoidtanh⁡(κ xiTxj+c)\tanh(\kappa\,x_i^Tx_j+c)tanh(κxiT​xj​+c), κ>0, c<0\kappa>0,\ c<0κ>0, c<0Proxy for neural networks (Mercer holds only for some parameters)
Graph / string / tree kernels—Similarity of graphs (bioinformatics), strings (text, genomes), trees (NLP)

7.8 Advantages and Disadvantages of SVM

Advantages
  • Classification and regression
  • Uses only a subset of the data (the support vectors) in the decision function, so it is memory-friendly
  • Works even in very high (even infinite) dimensions via kernels
  • Maximum margin gives good generalisation; convex, so there is one global optimum
  • Easier to use than neural networks
Disadvantages
  • Many parameters and kernels to choose (C, γ, kernel)
  • Slow to train on large datasets or with many features
  • Hard to interpret (“black box”)
  • No direct probability estimates
  • Sensitive to feature scaling

7.9 Solved Past Questions

2024 · Q3(a)Q7.1 — Define support vectors in Support Vector Machine (SVM). How is a decision boundary estimated from the SVM learning algorithm? Explain hard and soft margin.15Topic: SVM theory

Support vectors are the training points that lie closest to the decision boundary, exactly on the margin hyperplanes H1:wTx+b=+1H_1:w^Tx+b=+1H1​:wTx+b=+1 and H2:wTx+b=−1H_2:w^Tx+b=-1H2​:wTx+b=−1 (or inside the margin in the soft case). They satisfy yi(wTxi+b)=1y_i(w^Tx_i+b)=1yi​(wTxi​+b)=1 and have non-zero Lagrange multipliers αi>0\alpha_i>0αi​>0. They alone determine the hyperplane: moving any other point does not change the model. Draw Fig. 7.1.

How the decision boundary is estimated: (1) A hyperplane wTx+b=0w^Tx+b=0wTx+b=0 separates the classes, with the canonical constraint yi(wTxi+b)≥1y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\ge1yi​(wTxi​+b)≥1. (2) The margin width is 2/∥w∥2/\lVert w\rVert2/∥w∥, so maximising the margin means solving the primal min⁡12∥w∥2\min\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2min21​∥w∥2 subject to the constraints (§7.3). (3) Using Lagrange multipliers and KKT, this becomes the dual max⁡α∑αi−12∑∑αiαjyiyjxiTxj\max_\alpha\sum\alpha_i-\frac12\sum\sum\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_jx_i^Tx_jmaxα​∑αi​−21​∑∑αi​αj​yi​yj​xiT​xj​, s.t. αi≥0\alpha_i\ge0αi​≥0 (or ≤C\le C≤C), ∑αiyi=0\sum\alpha_iy_i=0∑αi​yi​=0 (§7.4), solved by quadratic programming. (4) Most αi\alpha_iαi​ come out as 0. The non-zero ones mark the support vectors. (5) Then w=∑αiyixiw=\sum\alpha_iy_ix_iw=∑αi​yi​xi​, b=ys−wTxsb=y_s-w^Tx_sb=ys​−wTxs​, and the classifier is f(x)=sign(wTx+b)f(x)=\mathrm{sign}(w^Tx+b)f(x)=sign(wTx+b). For non-linear data, replace xiTxjx_i^Tx_jxiT​xj​ by a kernel K(xi,xj)K(x_i,x_j)K(xi​,xj​).

Hard vs soft margin: the hard margin requires perfect linear separation with the widest margin: min⁡12∥w∥2\min\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2min21​∥w∥2, yi(wTxi+b)≥1y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\ge1yi​(wTxi​+b)≥1. It is suitable only for clean, separable data and is sensitive to outliers. The soft margin introduces slack variables ξi\xi_iξi​ and the penalty CCC: min⁡12∥w∥2+C∑ξi\min\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2+C\sum\xi_imin21​∥w∥2+C∑ξi​, yi(wTxi+b)≥1−ξiy_i(w^Tx_i+b)\ge1-\xi_iyi​(wTxi​+b)≥1−ξi​. It allows some violations, handles noise and overlap, and trades margin width against errors (large C: nearly hard margin; small C: wider margin, more errors). Include the comparison table of §7.5.

Source lectureAtia Ma'am · S5 – Support Vector Machines (MTE 4011 S5.pdf, pp. 6–25); S5 – Support Vector Machines (MTE 4011 S5.pdf, pp. 29–31)
2023 · Q3(a)Q7.2 — What are support vectors in support vector machine (SVM)? How does linear SVM works? Explain.10Topic: SVM theory

Support vectors: define them as in Q7.1. Working of linear SVM: (1) Represent the classes as y=±1y=\pm1y=±1 and look for a hyperplane wTx+b=0w^Tx+b=0wTx+b=0 (the lecture example x1+x2−5=0x_1+x_2-5=0x1​+x2​−5=0 shows how the sign of wTx+bw^Tx+bwTx+b decides the class). (2) Among all separating hyperplanes, choose the one with the maximum margin 2/∥w∥2/\lVert w\rVert2/∥w∥, subject to yi(wTxi+b)≥1y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\ge1yi​(wTxi​+b)≥1. (3) Solve min⁡12∥w∥2\min\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2min21​∥w∥2 via its Lagrangian dual (QP) to get the αi\alpha_iαi​. Non-zero αi\alpha_iαi​ identify the support vectors. (4) Compute w=∑αiyixiw=\sum\alpha_iy_ix_iw=∑αi​yi​xi​ and b=ys−wTxsb=y_s-w^Tx_sb=ys​−wTxs​. (5) Classify new points with sign(wTx+b)\mathrm{sign}(w^Tx+b)sign(wTx+b). (6) If the data overlaps, use the soft margin (slack ξi\xi_iξi​, parameter C). Draw Fig. 7.1.

2022 · Q2(a)Q7.3 — Consider the following optimization problem: Minimize f(x,y)=(x−1)2+(y−3)2f(x,y)=(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2f(x,y)=(x−1)2+(y−3)2 subject to x+y≤2x+y\le2x+y≤2, x≥yx\ge yx≥y. Write down the Lagrangian form for this problem.05Topic: Lagrangian / KKT
Given data
Objective f(x,y)=(x−1)2+(y−3)2f(x,y)=(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2f(x,y)=(x−1)2+(y−3)2. Constraints: x+y≤2x+y\le2x+y≤2 and x≥yx\ge yx≥y.
Step 1: Put the constraints in standard form gi≤0g_i\le0gi​≤0:
g1(x,y)=x+y−2≤0g_1(x,y)=x+y-2\le0g1​(x,y)=x+y−2≤0;   g2(x,y)=y−x≤0g_2(x,y)=y-x\le0g2​(x,y)=y−x≤0 (from x≥yx\ge yx≥y).
[SPECIAL SYMBOL / CONSTANT]“≥” constraints must be flipped to “≤ 0” form before attaching a non-negative multiplier.
Step 2: Lagrangian
L(x,y,μ1,μ2)=(x−1)2+(y−3)2+μ1(x+y−2)+μ2(y−x),μ1≥0, μ2≥0\mathcal{L}(x,y,\mu_1,\mu_2)=(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2+\mu_1(x+y-2)+\mu_2(y-x),\qquad \mu_1\ge0,\ \mu_2\ge0L(x,y,μ1​,μ2​)=(x−1)2+(y−3)2+μ1​(x+y−2)+μ2​(y−x),μ1​≥0, μ2​≥0
Step 3 (extra: solving with KKT). Stationarity: ∂L/∂x=2(x−1)+μ1−μ2=0\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x=2(x-1)+\mu_1-\mu_2=0∂L/∂x=2(x−1)+μ1​−μ2​=0, ∂L/∂y=2(y−3)+μ1+μ2=0\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial y=2(y-3)+\mu_1+\mu_2=0∂L/∂y=2(y−3)+μ1​+μ2​=0.
The unconstrained minimum (1, 3) violates both constraints (1+3=4>21+3=4>21+3=4>2 and 1<31<31<3), so try both active: x+y=2x+y=2x+y=2, x=yx=yx=y ⇒ (1,1)(1,1)(1,1).
Then 0+μ1−μ2=00+\mu_1-\mu_2=00+μ1​−μ2​=0 and −4+μ1+μ2=0-4+\mu_1+\mu_2=0−4+μ1​+μ2​=0 ⇒ μ1=μ2=2≥0\mu_1=\mu_2=2\ge0μ1​=μ2​=2≥0 ✓ (dual feasible). Optimum (x∗,y∗)=(1,1)(x^*,y^*)=(1,1)(x∗,y∗)=(1,1), f∗=4f^*=4f∗=4
[INTUITION]Positive multipliers mean both constraints are “pushing”: relaxing either would lower f. Checking one active constraint at a time gives infeasible points (0, 2) and (2, 2), which confirms the result.

Kernel: a function K(xi,xj)=ϕ(xi)Tϕ(xj)K(x_i,x_j)=\phi(x_i)^T\phi(x_j)K(xi​,xj​)=ϕ(xi​)Tϕ(xj​) that equals the dot product of two feature vectors after mapping them into a higher-dimensional feature space by ϕ\phiϕ. It measures their similarity in that space without computing ϕ\phiϕ explicitly (the kernel trick), which lets a linear SVM learn non-linear boundaries. In the dual, xiTxjx_i^Tx_jxiT​xj​ is replaced by K(xi,xj)K(x_i,x_j)K(xi​,xj​). Give the (xTz)2(x^Tz)^2(xTz)2 example of §7.7.

Mercer's condition: a symmetric function KKK is a valid kernel if and only if it is positive semi-definite: ∑i∑jcicjK(xi,xj)≥0\sum_i\sum_jc_ic_jK(x_i,x_j)\ge0∑i​∑j​ci​cj​K(xi​,xj​)≥0 for any points and any real constants cic_ici​ (every Gram matrix is PSD). Functions satisfying it can be expressed as a dot product in some high-dimensional space.

Three kernels: (1) Polynomial K=(xiTxj+1)dK=(x_i^Tx_j+1)^dK=(xiT​xj​+1)d: includes all feature interactions up to degree d, used for curved boundaries. (2) Gaussian RBF K=exp⁡(−∥xi−xj∥2/2σ2)K=\exp(-\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert^2/2\sigma^2)K=exp(−∥xi​−xj​∥2/2σ2): similarity decays with distance and gives an infinite-dimensional mapping. It is the most popular general-purpose kernel, with σ controlling smoothness. (3) Sigmoid / hyperbolic tangent K=tanh⁡(κxiTxj+c)K=\tanh(\kappa x_i^Tx_j+c)K=tanh(κxiT​xj​+c): behaves like a two-layer neural network. (Also: linear xiTxjx_i^Tx_jxiT​xj​, Laplace RBF, string/graph/tree kernels.)
